title: IB French B Extended Response: Plan, Write, Check
summary: IB French B extended response guide: decode prompts, plan in two minutes, structure your writing, and check assessment criteria before timed exam practice.
body_markdown:
An **IB French B extended response** succeeds when it answers every part of the task, develops relevant ideas, and uses French suited to its audience and text type. Under time pressure, the most useful routine is straightforward: decode the prompt, make a two-minute plan, write with a clear purpose, and check against the assessment criteria.


Here, “extended response” means the longer writing task in Paper 1. For the course assessed before the revised syllabus first assessment in May 2029, SL students write 250-400 words in 75 minutes; HL students write 450-600 words in 90 minutes. Check which syllabus applies to your examination session.


The challenge is making several decisions while the clock keeps moving. A repeatable process makes those decisions easier.


### Your IB French B extended response checklist


Before writing, establish five things:


- **Purpose:** What must this text achieve?
- **Audience:** Who will read it?
- **Content:** Which instructions must you address?
- **Text type:** Which offered option best suits the task?
- **Register:** How formal should the French sound?


Keep these visible in your planning notes. They connect your writing decisions to the marks available. For broader assessment context, consult RevisionDojo’s[IB Language B paper format guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/a-comprehensive-guide-to-the-ib-language-b-paper-format) .


### Decode the question before choosing your vocabulary


Imagine a practice task asking you to write to your headteacher about reducing waste at school. You must explain the problem, propose changes, and persuade the school to act.


The topic is waste. The task is persuasion directed at someone with authority. That distinction determines what belongs in the response.


Underline the instruction verbs and turn them into actions:


- **Explain:** Show why waste is a problem at your school.
- **Propose:** Give practical measures the school could introduce.
- **Persuade:** Explain the benefits and make a clear request.


Then identify your relationship with the reader. A letter to a headteacher needs a respectful register and appropriate opening and closing conventions. A speech to classmates needs direct audience engagement.


Choose among the text types actually offered. Familiarity helps, but the format still needs to fit the purpose. A polished diary entry would struggle to fulfil a task requiring a formal proposal to school leadership.


### Build a two-minute plan


Two minutes is a useful planning target once you have selected and decoded the task. It is a practice technique, not an IB requirement.


### First minute: map the content


Write one short note for each required element. For the hypothetical waste task:


- Problem: disposable packaging fills classroom bins.
- Proposal: introduce refill stations and reusable containers.
- Persuasion: explain practical benefits and suggest a trial period.


These notes give each paragraph a job. If the prompt contains another instruction, add another note. Never let a convenient three-paragraph formula erase part of the task.


### Second minute: choose usable French


Add a few phrases you can use accurately:


- *Nous constatons que…* to introduce an observation.
- *Il serait souhaitable de…* to propose action politely.
- *Cette mesure permettrait de…* to explain a benefit.
- *Certes…, cependant…* to acknowledge a difficulty.


Choose vocabulary you understand well enough to adapt. Planning an impressive expression creates little value if you cannot use it clearly in the sentence you need.


A student points to a clock while a tiny crowned figure standing on dictionaries suggests a fancy synonym.


### Structure the response around the reader


Good **IB French B essay technique** starts with recognising that Paper 1 may require a letter, article, speech, or another text type. A generic academic essay structure will not suit every option.


Open by establishing the situation and purpose. For the imagined formal letter, a suitable opening might be:


*Madame la Directrice, je vous écris pour proposer plusieurs mesures visant à réduire les déchets dans notre établissement.*


The reader immediately knows why you are writing.


Develop each main paragraph through an idea, an explanation, and a relevant detail. For example, proposing refill stations becomes more convincing when you explain how they could reduce disposable bottle use and where they might be installed.


Avoid invented statistics. A plausible example can support your reasoning without pretending to be research.


Finish with an ending appropriate to the format: a request in a letter, a recommendation in an article, or a call to action in a speech. RevisionDojo’s[guide to achieving a 7 in French B](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-french-b) provides a wider framework for practising these writing skills.


### Use the assessment criteria while writing


For the pre-2029 Paper 1 framework, the response is assessed through Language, Message, and Conceptual understanding, worth 12, 12, and 6 marks respectively.


**Language:** Use relevant vocabulary and a range of grammatical structures with control. Complexity helps when it communicates your meaning accurately. A conditional recommendation is useful because the task calls for a proposal.


**Message:** Address every instruction and develop your ideas. Naming three solutions gives the reader less substance than explaining how each could work and why it matters.


**Conceptual understanding:** Maintain an appropriate text type, register, tone, and recognisable conventions. A formal greeting cannot compensate for an otherwise casual letter.


During practice, turn these criteria into questions: Is my French clear? Have I developed the required content? Does this sound appropriate for this reader?


### Protect time for checking


For practice, try this allocation: five minutes to select, decode, and plan; 62 minutes to write at SL or 77 at HL; and eight minutes to check. Adjust it as you learn your writing pace.


Check content first. Missing a required proposal can matter more than one incorrect adjective ending.


Then check text conventions and register, followed by recurring language errors: verb endings, agreement, articles, accents, and tense consistency. Finally, check the required word range. Estimate length periodically rather than counting every word while composing.


### Turn one timed response into better preparation


After an **IB French B long answer** , record one weakness under each assessment criterion. Rewrite the weakest paragraph before starting another full response. This makes feedback practical.


Use RevisionDojo’s[French B resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-french-b) to organise subject practice, and its[French B self-study guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-french-b-resources-self-study) to build a manageable routine.


Then practise task selection and writing in the[Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/questionbank) , and sit timed papers in Exam mode. The aim is to make the process familiar: understand the reader, plan the message, develop it clearly, and leave time to check.
